sections.title: Choose your starting point
sections.body:
GopherForge brings two useful workflows together: a native Go workbench for iPhone and iPad, and a learning library you can also read in a browser. The app bundles Go 1.27.1. It compiles on your device; running a small program does not require an account or a remote execution service. The website provides free lessons, interview preparation and a Go Playground that compiles and executes locally in a browser worker. Neither workflow uploads code to a remote compiler. Creating a shared room explicitly uploads its selected source to the relay.

Start with **Projects** if you have an idea to build. Start with **Learn → Course** if you want a structured path through the language. Choose **Learn → Interview** to practice explanations, tradeoffs and algorithms. You can move between these areas without treating an interview self-assessment as course completion.

The current web course has **229 teaching lessons, 182 readings and 22 prediction challenges across 29 units**, plus **132 interview guides and 12 algorithm walkthroughs**. Native **1.3.3 (55)** is available in private Internal QA TestFlight. On first native use, explicitly download a complete **Go**, **DevOps** or **Interview** course from **Learn → Course downloads**. Opening a lesson never fetches its content. The DevOps area includes 34 readings in four units, six local terminal labs and a free shell playground. The public App Store version remains **1.3.2 (51)** with bundled learning content. Check [version history](/updates) before relying on a native-only feature.

sections.title: Your first fifteen minutes
sections.body:
Open **Projects → Create new project** and choose a small template. Give it a meaningful name, then open its main Go file. Read the package declaration and imports before changing the program. Change one visible output string, tap **Run**, and compare the result in Output with your expectation. The first build can take longer while the bundled tools prepare their working files.

Next, add a small function with a clear input and return value. Add a test file ending in `_test.go`, then run **Test**. Make the test fail deliberately once, fix the implementation and rerun it. This gives you a reliable distinction between a successful compilation and a checked behavior.

Finish by formatting the project. Export a copy through the project controls before making a larger experiment. A useful first session is one small program you understand, one test you can explain, and a copy you know how to find again.

sections.title: Files, editing and screen space
sections.body:
Inside Build, the **Files** control opens or closes the project navigator. Use it to select another source file, inspect the module file or add project content. Files is a collapsible sidebar; it does not need to remain open while you write. The active file appears above the editor so you can confirm where a change will go.

The editor provides Go syntax highlighting, line numbers and a coding accessory for touch input. With an external keyboard, the touch accessory should not reserve an empty keyboard-sized area. You can scroll past the final source line to keep the last lines clear of floating navigation; that extra space is visual padding, not text inserted into your file.

Layouts adapt to iPhone, iPad and supported Duo postures. If a problem appears only after rotating or changing posture, record the orientation, keyboard state and active pane. [Support](/support) explains the details that make a layout report reproducible.

sections.title: Build, run, test, vet and format
sections.body:
These operations answer different questions. **Build** checks and links the program. **Run** builds and executes the main package. **Test** executes package tests. **Vet** reports suspicious constructs that can compile successfully. **Format** rewrites source with the bundled formatter. A clean build alone does not prove that your program is correct.

Use Problems to locate diagnostics and Output to read execution results. Read the first relevant error before fixing every later message: a missing import or malformed declaration can cause several downstream reports. When a setup or dependency step fails, the program may not have started at all.

The workbench runs a bounded WASI environment. It is appropriate for compatible pure-Go programs, learning exercises and local project experiments. It does not provide arbitrary native system calls, cgo, native assembly or guest-program networking. In an ordinary run, an infinite loop has no guaranteed Stop; an unresponsive run may require closing and reopening the app. Keep important source exported.

sections.title: Use the project console deliberately
sections.body:
Terminal is an app-scoped project console. It maps supported commands to the workbench’s existing operations. It is useful when you prefer a command-oriented view of a project, but it is not a general shell or a remote machine.

```text
help
go build
go run
go test
go vet
go fmt
go mod
ls
cat main.go
pwd
clear
```

`go mod` displays the parsed module. It does not expose every desktop `go mod` subcommand. Likewise, this console does not promise arbitrary flags, shell pipelines, Bash scripts, SSH sessions or Kubernetes administration. The Around Go lessons show commands for a separate native development environment; reading those commands does not install those tools into the app.

If a command is rejected, check `help` and the corresponding toolbar operation. Avoid repeatedly submitting an unsupported desktop workflow and interpreting the response as a Go language failure.

sections.title: Build React offline with the npm command subset
sections.body:
**Available in 1.3.1 (49).** This mode lets you study a browser interface beside your Go source without sending the project to a build server. Start with **Projects → Examples → Offline frontend → React + Gin study board**. Open Terminal, then run:

```text
frontend packages
npm install --offline
npm run build
frontend preview
```

Select **Output → Open full screen**. Add tasks, change filters and inspect the project’s components, TypeScript model and CSS. Edit a component and rebuild to compare the result. Source, the offline lock and generated assets are autosaved; browser state is temporary. A source edit invalidates the old preview so it is not silently presented as a current build.

This is an educational npm command subset backed by bundled esbuild WASI, React / React DOM 19.3.1 and scheduler 0.28.0. It handles browser JS, JSX, TS, TSX, CSS and local JSON imports. TypeScript is transpiled without type checking. `npm ci --offline` checks an existing matching offline lock; `npm run preview` is also supported when its script is the documented GopherForge preview command.

It is not a full npm or Node.js installation. Arbitrary package scripts, lifecycle hooks, native addons, Node server APIs, Vite plugins, registry downloads and Bun are unavailable. Package scripts must be `gopherforge build` or `gopherforge preview`; `gopherforge.frontend.json` is declarative data, not executable configuration. Only the fixed bundled catalog is accepted. Missing packages fail explicitly instead of reaching the internet.

The compiler works inside a fresh bounded WASI tree. Generated code runs in nonpersistent WebKit storage on a project-specific origin. External HTTP(S), WebSockets, workers, frames and popups are blocked in this isolated frontend mode. There is no TCP listener or remote execution service. GitHub import and missing Go dependencies still need a connection before offline work begins. See [supported local Go APIs](#local-go-api) and [package compatibility](/support#package-limits) before importing a larger project.

**Included in 1.3.1 (49):** Output also offers **Build & Preview** when generated assets are missing or stale, including after a successful Go Run. It uses the same offline install/build pipeline as Terminal and shows errors in place. The embedded viewer adds **Reload** and **Share project…** alongside full screen. Sharing sends the project archive, not a public website or temporary browser state. The isolated custom origin remains available only inside GopherForge.

sections.title: Connect a teaching React interface to local Go handlers
sections.body:
**Included in 1.3.1 (49):** a small deterministic in-memory Go API can serve an isolated React preview through the educational Gin-compatible adapter. This is useful for tracing a form’s JSON request, Go validation, state changes and the response that updates a component. The built-in study board itself uses a local JSON fixture; opt into real handlers explicitly for your own compatible project.

Start from the Gin-compatible template, keep its vendored teaching adapter, and configure explicit local prefixes in `gopherforge.frontend.json`:

```json
{
  "entry": "web/src/main.tsx",
  "html": "web/index.html",
  "output": "web/dist",
  "minify": true,
  "backend": "gin-replay",
  "backendPaths": ["/api/items"]
}
```

Browser `fetch('/api/items')` calls then reach real Go handlers through a bounded main-frame bridge and `httptest`. The adapter supports GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE, named path parameters, JSON binding and JSON responses. It is a subset, not the complete Gin framework or an arbitrary long-running server.

Each request starts a fresh WASI execution. Earlier mutations are replayed first to reconstruct deterministic in-memory state, then the new handler runs. The linked Go program is cached. Embedded and full-screen previews share the API session; rebuilding or reopening the project resets it. GET handlers should be read-only. Time, randomness, background workers, external services, database transactions and streaming do not have general server semantics here.

Budgets are explicit: up to 16 local path prefixes, 32 KiB per request body, 64 mutations per session, 2 MiB of encoded history and 256 KiB per response body. Reads remain available after the mutation limit. A limit produces an explanation rather than silently starting a network service. The usual Go guest memory budgets still apply.

An external React + Gin GitHub project was used to verify real read/create/update/delete operations and network blocking. Its source and its example are not bundled in GopherForge. The feature is the local build and API capability; imported projects remain subject to dependency and WASI compatibility. [Technical documentation](https://github.com/sergii-ziborov/GopherForge/blob/codex/datastores-and-scroll/docs/OFFLINE_FRONTEND.md) includes the recipe, limits and reproducible verification records.

sections.title: Set a breakpoint: Run chooses the debugger automatically
sections.body:
**Included in 1.3.1 (49):** tap a Go line number to set a red breakpoint, then use the usual **Run** button. **Without breakpoints, Run executes normally. With breakpoints, it automatically starts the source debugger.** The file header also has controls to toggle a breakpoint at the caret and remove all breakpoints. Their positions persist per project on this device.

Try **Examples → Source debugger → Source debugger walkthrough**. Set a breakpoint on line 12, `result := double(start)`. Run stops before the call with `start = 3`. **Step Into** enters `double` at line 6 and shows `n = 3`. **Step Over** reaches its return with `value = 6`. **Step Out** returns to line 13 with `result = 6`. **Continue** finishes and displays `6` in Output; **Stop** ends the session.

The panel shows the current goroutine, an instrumented project call stack, the executing source location and bounded current-frame local values. Select a stack frame to reveal its source. Large collections show type/length/capacity summaries instead of expanding unbounded data. Caller-frame locals are not captured. A blank-line breakpoint binds to the next executable statement in its file; if there is none, the app asks you to move it.

The original source compiles first. Trusted checkpoints are then inserted into a temporary snapshot for the debug run. Saved source is never overwritten, and the ordinary execution cache stays separate. The editor is read-only while debugging; switching projects or changing source stops the session. The compiler worker pauses while the UI remains responsive.

This is a beta teaching source debugger. Vendor and standard-library code are not stepped. Conditional/data breakpoints, watch expressions, variable mutation, a full goroutine inspector and live stdout streaming are absent. Stop takes effect at the next project checkpoint; an unreturning call inside uninstrumented dependency code cannot be interrupted by a source probe. Instrumentation changes timing and allocations, so use ordinary runs and native development tools for performance or race analysis. [Release details](/updates#v130) record the availability of each native build.

sections.title: Import, export and keep projects findable
sections.body:
You can create projects from templates, import a GitHub repository, or open compatible content from Files. GitHub import requires a connection. Review the imported tree and `go.mod` before building an unfamiliar project, especially when it has a large dependency graph or expects native operating-system services.

Projects stay on the device unless you choose a location in Files or iCloud Drive. The project library can be kept in a selected folder; individual projects can also be exported as folders or archives. A folder provider being available in Files is separate from a complete build being supported by the compiler sandbox.

Use a small library with descriptive project names rather than several indistinguishable template copies. Export before deleting or reorganizing a project. The app does not automatically upload source to a coding-agent provider, and the website does not share your native project library. [Package compatibility](/support#package-limits) is the next check when an imported repository fails before compilation.

sections.title: Organize projects, examples and the file tree
sections.body:
On **Projects**, create a project, browse Examples, search your library or use the project organizer to change its name, folder, comma-separated tags, summary and favorite mark. Library folders organize projects; folders inside Build organize one project's source. Give similar experiments distinct names and summaries so you can find the right copy before exporting or deleting it.

Use the navigator inside Build to select, create, rename or remove files and folders. Check the active file header before editing. Go package declarations and import paths must still agree with the source directory: moving a file in the tree does not automatically redesign its imports. `go.mod` controls the module; generated output is separate from saved source.

**Examples** includes ready-made Go experiments, an offline React study board and a source-debugger walkthrough. Starting from an example creates an editable project. Read its description and expected output first; an example that uses the educational Gin adapter does not become a full network server.

For Files/iCloud, open a compatible folder or `.tar.gz` archive from Projects, or choose a folder to hold the project library. **Settings → Projects → Open on-device library** returns to the local library when a chosen folder is active. Existing libraries open in place. Switching waits for the current edit to save; save/bookmark errors require attention. Keep both independently exported copies when resolving a provider conflict. See [source safety and import details](#audit-beta).

sections.title: Dependencies, offline work and archive limits
sections.body:
Automatic dependency preparation uses requirements already declared in `go.mod`. Once compatible source is present, later builds can use it without downloading it again. Importing a repository or fetching missing packages still needs a connection. This is not a full desktop module-version solver, and `go.work` semantics are not implemented.

GopherForge applies independent resource budgets to downloaded module archives:

| Budget | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 4,000 files | Non-directory ZIP entries, counted before source filtering |
| 96 MiB compressed | Maximum download size of one module ZIP |
| 512 MiB uncompressed | Maximum expanded size of one module |
| 80 modules | Maximum dependencies prepared in one pass |

These are application budgets, not Go language limits. Tests, documentation and other-platform sources count toward the ZIP entry budget even when they will later be discarded. For example, `modernc.org/libc@v1.75.3` has 4,168 files and is rejected during Setup. Retry cannot make that same archive smaller.

Passing an archive check also does not establish WASI compatibility. Non-Go `go:embed` assets are not generally preserved by vendoring. Read [the detailed limits](/support#package-limits) before changing dependency versions or assuming that SQLite-based applications will run.

sections.title: Local web previews, pictures and diagnostic tools
sections.body:
The workbench can present compatible local HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a WebKit preview and display PNG output from Go programs. These are useful for small visual experiments: generate an image, inspect it, then change one parameter and run again. A preview is not evidence that a guest Go HTTP server can open a network listener.

The Gin-style templates use a bundled educational compatibility layer, not the complete upstream Gin framework. They exercise registered handlers through `httptest`; the native app serves the resulting local preview. This does not run an arbitrary live Go backend. The App Store 1.3.1 workbench includes these static previews. Its [offline frontend mode](#offline-react) adds isolated browser builds with a documented npm command subset, and [explicit local API paths](#local-go-api) can execute compatible Go handlers. Full Node.js/npm and Bun are not bundled. Projects outside the fixed catalog still need an external frontend build; database-backed services belong in that native external environment.

Legacy local HTML or JavaScript previews can contact remote services referenced by that content. The new isolated frontend mode instead blocks external requests. This differs from networking inside the sandboxed Go program. Inspect imported web content and external resource URLs if you want a fully local experiment.

Concurrency Lab provides nine modeled scenarios for reasoning about goroutines and synchronization. Idiom Coach applies deterministic rules to source. They are learning aids, not a production runtime trace or an AI code review service. Use compiler tests and a native race detector when you validate real concurrent software. The [concurrency unit](/learn/units/concurrency) explains cancellation, joining and modern test tools.

**Included in 1.3.1 (49):** legacy static previews offer **Open in Browser**, **Share local address**, and **Share project…**. A loopback URL works only on the device running the preview; iOS may suspend it after an app switch. The port printed by a Gin exercise is not an internet endpoint. To give another person the files, share the archive. Isolated React previews retain their app-only WebKit origin and do not expose an external browser URL.

sections.title: Follow the course without losing your place
sections.body:
**Native 1.3.3 (55):** use **Learn → Course downloads** to install the entire Go, DevOps or Interview course before studying. Export a complete file for later offline import. Removing course content keeps your progress, bookmarks, drafts and lab files. New revisions require another explicit complete download.

The course combines editable exercises, prediction challenges and worked readings. In an exercise, make a small change and run the check. A compiler-verified completion records evidence from execution. A reading can be marked complete without invoking the compiler; that mark means you finished studying it, not that an arbitrary implementation passed tests.

**Continue where you left off** returns to the saved course lesson. Go, DevOps and Interview keep separate places. Native progress is stored locally and survives normal app relaunches. Keep that distinction in mind before deleting the app or its data: local persistence is not a promise of account-based cloud recovery.

On the website, progress and bookmarks live in browser storage. Return in the same browser and device to see your saved place. Clearing site data, private browsing or storage restrictions can remove or prevent that record. Browser progress and app progress are independent.

A sensible route is [Go core](/learn/units/core), collections, errors and modules, followed by concurrency and the design topics that match your project. You do not need to read every architecture before writing a useful small program.

**In 1.3.1 (49):** your editable lesson draft and your own text before inserting the solution are saved locally and restored after a process relaunch. Continue returns to the lesson; draft restoration returns the code. Reset affects the draft only after confirmation. Changed lesson content and save failures are explained. Hint/solution assistance is stored separately from compiler evidence. Course and unit pages expose Practice directly, including Lab formats.

In compiler exercises, **Inspect and edit verification source** opens `main.go` and `lesson_test.go` in a separate experiment. You can inspect or change either file and run experimental tests. Those edits cannot award an official compiler-verified course pass; the original course checks retain their verified source.

sections.title: Review, fix mistakes and understand the badges
sections.body:
**Review** asks you to connect learned ideas with their meanings. It builds matching pairs from eligible completed material rather than marking a new course lesson complete on your behalf. Complete a few distinct lessons if the review board has no learned pairs yet.

**Fix mistakes** revisits concepts with a question and three alternatives. After an incorrect answer, read the explanation and compare it with the misconception you chose. A correct response supplies new evidence for that concept. The purpose is to repair a misunderstanding, not to unlock a sequence merely by tapping a checkmark.

Achievements summarize learning events. They are not professional certifications, and a self-reported reading mark should not be confused with compiler evidence. When a topic feels familiar, explain it without the answer visible, then use a code example or prediction challenge to test that explanation. [JSON input policy](/learn/stdlib.json-input-policy) is a useful example of a subject where recognizing a function name is much easier than defining a reliable contract.

Open **Learn → Practice** for prediction challenges, matching drills, quizzes, Spot the Bug, interview questions and compiler exercises, grouped by course unit. These formats are available directly; finishing a lesson is not an unlock requirement. **Concurrency Lab** is also linked there. Choose a scenario, predict the next event, then step through the modeled timeline and compare goroutine state. Its nine scenarios illustrate scheduling and synchronization; they do not trace the runtime behavior of your arbitrary project.

sections.title: Prepare for a Go developer interview
sections.body:
The expanded Interview library contains 132 worked guides across 15 topics and four difficulty levels, from junior foundations to staff-level tradeoffs. Read the prompt first, speak your answer aloud, then compare the reasoning, trap and follow-up. Mark whether you understand the topic or want to revisit it. That self-assessment stays separate from course completion.

The twelve interactive algorithm labs contain 36 scenarios. Step through the state changes before reading the final result. New labs cover [topological sorting](/interview/algorithms.topological-sort), [union-find](/interview/algorithms.union-find), [LRU eviction](/interview/algorithms.lru-cache) and [merging intervals](/interview/algorithms.merge-intervals), alongside search, windows, heaps, graphs and other fundamentals.

Do not memorize only the displayed code. Explain input assumptions, ownership, time and space complexity, empty inputs and failure cases. For an LRU cache, distinguish entry capacity from a byte budget and a recency policy from a time-to-live policy. For a dependency graph, explain what a cycle means to the caller. Those boundaries often matter more than the short implementation.

sections.title: Move from examples to real Go services
sections.body:
Around Go connects language knowledge to a working environment. The library covers Bash and Git, modules and tooling, Docker, Kubernetes, MongoDB and Redis. The new SQL unit explains connection pools, row ownership, transaction boundaries, isolation, locking and retry safety. Its examples target a native Go service with a database; the iPhone sandbox does not become a database server or network-enabled SQL client.

The coding-agent unit covers Go workflows with Codex, Claude Code and Cursor: repository guidance, small reviewable changes, API verification, tests and trust boundaries. These are instructions for using external development tools. GopherForge does not bundle an agent subscription, send your project to those providers or execute their commands for you.

Start with [the agent workflow](/learn/ai.go-workflow), then [verify generated Go](/learn/ai.verify-generated-go). For database work, begin with [pool lifetime](/learn/sql.pool-lifetime) and [transaction ownership](/learn/sql.transaction-owner). Use the linked official references and test the examples against the actual toolchain, driver and service versions you deploy.

The [Gin services unit](/learn/units/gin) covers middleware order, bounded binding, pooled request contexts, trusted proxies, error mapping and graceful shutdown. [Blockchain infrastructure](/learn/units/blockchain) covers go-ethereum, Bitcoin and Cosmos package roles, exact token amounts, RPC deadlines, ABI calls, nonce ownership, signer boundaries and reorg-safe indexing. These are development lessons, not a wallet or a new guest-networking capability. Full Gin and protocol SDK examples run in a native Go environment; local preview still uses the app’s teaching adapter.

[System design](/learn/units/system-design) and [clean code in production](/learn/units/clean-code-production) add transaction ownership, outbox/inbox, sagas, compatible rollout, tenant isolation, telemetry, gRPC, Kafka and consistency choices. Start with a failure case and explain the recovery contract before selecting a pattern.

sections.title: Settings, privacy and a useful next step
sections.body:
Settings controls appearance, editor text size, screen-awake behavior and supported project-library preferences. The About section identifies the installed version and build. Include those values in a bug report; they are more useful than assuming every TestFlight or App Store installation contains the latest website material.

The native app is a one-time paid purchase with no subscription or in-app purchases. The website shows a launch offer: **$6.99 USD, reduced from $9.99**; the App Store shows the final price for your region. The web course is freely readable. The app does not include advertising or third-party analytics SDKs. The website has separate infrastructure analytics; see [Privacy](/privacy) for the distinction.

If you are new to GopherForge, finish one lesson and return through Continue. If you already write Go, build a small project and test an edge case you normally overlook. Then choose one interview guide and explain its tradeoff to another person. The value is a repeatable loop: read, predict, run, inspect and revise. For a problem you cannot resolve, [contact support](/support) with a minimal example and the exact diagnostic.

sections.title: Settings, Face ID and storage maintenance
sections.body:
Open **Settings** for the controls below. Changes to appearance and text size affect presentation; they do not alter Go source or reset learning progress.

| Control | Use and effect |
| --- | --- |
| Theme | Choose the available appearance mode |
| Text size | Set the source editor from 11 to 22 pt |
| Keep the screen awake | Control idle behavior; builds and package downloads already keep the screen awake |
| Require Face ID | Authenticate before enabling; Face ID or the device passcode is required when returning to the app |
| Toolchain | Inspect readiness, the bundled Go version, size and execution limits |
| Clear build cache | Remove compiled programs; the next run recompiles from saved source |
| Clear downloaded packages | Remove dependency source from saved projects; your source and declared versions stay, and packages need downloading again |
| Reset learning progress | Confirm removal of lesson, drill, quiz and mistake-correction records |
| About | Find the installed version/build, notices and support information |

App lock controls access when returning to the native app. It does not encrypt a shared Playground room or revoke previously shared links. Downloads can continue beneath the lock. Do not confuse clearing a compiled-program cache with deleting your projects, and export browser progress separately before clearing browser storage.

Before resetting progress, read the confirmation carefully: the reset is not a way to refresh a missing lesson. If a bundled compiler reports a problem, record its status and installed version first. If a provider folder is unavailable, restore its access rather than substituting a new empty project library.

sections.title: Recover from a failed run, missing work or stale output
sections.body:
**Setup fails before your program starts:** read the first dependency/import error and check [module budgets](#modules). A repeat of the same oversized archive does not change its compatibility. In browser Playground, declare an exact version in `go.mod`, then choose Packages → Prepare packages. Run reuses the verified prepared tree. A changed `go.mod` or `go.sum` requires preparing again.

**A build or test fails:** open Problems in the app or click the browser diagnostic. Start with the earliest relevant source error. A Test failure can be a valid execution that found the behavior you asked it to check. Compare the expected value, observed output and source revision before editing.

**A program loops forever:** use browser **Stop**; the worker is also subject to its deadline. In an ordinary native run, Stop for arbitrary tight loops is not guaranteed. A source-debugger Stop takes effect at a project checkpoint. If native execution cannot finish, closing and reopening the app may be necessary; export important source before risky experiments.

**Output looks unchanged:** check its source revision and rebuild after editing. A browser result marked older source is not evidence for your new draft. A React preview invalidated by an edit needs Build & Preview. Local handler state and temporary browser preview state reset after their documented session boundaries.

**A room disconnects or expires:** the current local draft remains available. Export a ZIP or save an independent native project, then create/join a new room. Expired links and closed rooms cannot be revived by repeatedly reconnecting. If edits conflict, download your draft before loading shared source. A relay restart can end a one-hour room early.

**A lesson or project appears missing:** check which Files library, browser profile, device and app build you opened. Native and web progress are independent. Continue stores a place; completing a reading, passing a compiler check and marking an interview topic are different records. For web progress recovery use its exported backup; a published read-only progress link does not automatically restore local state.

Contact [Support](/support) with the installed version/build, device/browser, exact operation, minimal source, complete diagnostic and source revision when sharing a room result. For layout problems add orientation, keyboard type and active pane. Keep capability links and private project data out of public reports.

sections.title: Back up and move your browser progress
sections.body:
On Learn Go or Interview, open **Back up or move your local progress**. Download the JSON file before clearing browser data or moving to another browser. It contains only course completion marks, interview self-assessments and Continue bookmarks. It excludes unrelated browser storage, project secrets, Git credentials and temporary sharing links.

Choose a saved file to preview its date, content revision, new marks, existing matches and unknown material IDs. Nothing changes until you select **Merge into this browser**. Existing marks and current Continue positions stay; incoming marks fill gaps. When interview answers conflict, this browser’s existing self-assessment stays. Unknown material IDs are skipped and listed, so keep the original file for a future catalog. An older or poorer backup does not erase newer work.

This is a manual web-to-web transfer. It does not claim native app synchronization, cloud backup or compiler verification. Storage quota errors leave the previous imported state intact. Files with an unsupported schema or a combined history above this version’s record limit are refused. Your browser data remains local; no registration or upload service is involved.

sections.title: Source safety, Files libraries and import details
sections.body:
**GopherForge 1.3.1 (49)** introduced source-safety changes, restored lesson drafts and direct Practice access. Native Playground and progress publishing were added separately in 1.3.2 (51), now available on the App Store. [Version history](/updates) records the public and beta states.

In this version, opening an existing library in Files opens that library instead of replacing its contents. Switching libraries waits for the open source to save. Conflicting edits are preserved as separately named projects. Test with disposable libraries on your actual Files/iCloud provider, keep independent exports and compare both copies before deleting anything. The local Apple Files-provider flow was checked on a physical iPhone: two separate libraries, edits, switching and process relaunch retained their own source. Remote iCloud synchronization and arbitrary third-party providers remain separate verification tasks. An unreadable saved bookmark or a missing known library now reports a failure instead of silently substituting the on-device library.

GitHub imports resolve a requested branch or tag to a fixed commit before downloading. UTF-8 fixtures, vendor source, CI and React/TypeScript files are retained within limits. **Project → Import details** records the selected scope, retained paths, omissions and archive identity. This is a bounded text snapshot, not a complete worktree: binary assets and Git history are not reconstructed by export. Old unpinned imports do not silently receive files from today’s moving branch.

The console rejects unsupported terminal flags and targets rather than running a different command. Idiom Apply reviews the exact target file and refuses stale source; transformations that cannot be demonstrated safe remain advice. Settings states that memory and captured output are bounded, while a universal native Stop and an aggregate guest file-write quota are not guaranteed.

sections.title: MCP Playground and sharing learning progress
sections.body:
Use **Compatible** rooms for remote MCP clients and App Store 1.3.2. The browser now asks for your nickname before creating or joining; that display label appears beside your cursor, in participants, recent changes and new run results. It is not an authenticated identity. Native nickname prompts and these new controls are included in **1.3.3 (55), in private TestFlight**.

Choose **Share → Room type → Compatible · iPhone/iPad and remote MCP** for the protocol described in this section. Browser-only participants can instead use the [encrypted live room](#browser-collaboration).

The [shared Playground](/playground) supports Go execution in your browser as well as collaboration with compatible native builds. Follow the [browser walkthrough](#browser-playground) for local execution and the [MCP setup guide](/guide/mcp) to connect Claude, Codex or another supported remote MCP client. Native room support is available in App Store 1.3.2 (51). Update an older installation before joining a room.

An assistant can call `playground_join` with a nickname, retain its returned participant capability, read the room, publish a revision-checked source edit and request a run. **A person presses Run/Test in their browser or the native app.** No incoming edit, room link, AI request or reconnection automatically runs code. Results identify the reporting device and captured revision; older-source output remains labelled as such. Other participants receive the result without executing that code themselves. The relay has no compiler or shell.

Create a room to upload the current file set. Share **Edit** for source changes or **View** for reading. View participants can run their own local browser copy but cannot change shared source or publish room results. Keep the Owner key in the creating tab; it can close the room. A collaborator's pending request appears beside Output. Review the code, then deliberately choose Run or Test. Save an independent native project copy or export a ZIP before the room ends.

On Learn or Interview, publish a read-only 90-day progress snapshot for a teacher or assistant. It includes marks and Continue places, excludes source and drafts, does not update automatically and can be revoked from the publishing device. Publishing progress is separate from exporting its local backup.

Rooms normally expire after one hour and may end earlier after a relay restart. Anyone holding a link has its role until expiry or closure. In this compatible mode, the relay can read shared source and Output; this mode does not provide end-to-end encryption. Conflicting whole-file edits are rejected rather than silently merged. Download the kept draft, load the latest source and reapply your intended changes. Native builds retain their own documented execution limits; the browser's Stop and 30-second deadline do not change native Run.

sections.title: Browser Playground: a complete local Go workspace
sections.body:
Open [Playground](/playground). A local Hello, Go draft is ready without registration or an app installation. Choose **Run** or press **Ctrl/⌘ + Enter**. On first use, approximately 47 MiB of compressed Go/WASI tools and standard-library archives download from this site. The files are SHA-256 verified and cached when browser storage allows. Your source stays on this device until you explicitly create or join a room and publish it. Revisiting the website still requires the page to be available; cached compiler assets alone are not an offline-installed web app.

Use **Open an example** for a simple program, standard input, functions with tests or multiple packages. Replacing a draft asks for confirmation. Use the explorer’s **New file / New folder** buttons with a relative path such as `mathx/double.go`; source in a folder forms a separate Go package. Rename an individual file or enter its folder path to move that folder's files. Delete removes the active file after confirmation. Keep `main.go` at the root. The `module` directive in `go.mod` defines imports such as `playground/mathx`.

The editor has syntax highlighting, line numbers, folding, matching brackets, indentation, undo and find/replace. **Ctrl/⌘ + F** opens search. Click a compiler diagnostic below Output to jump to its file and line. Edits are stored locally; private browsing, storage restrictions or clearing site data can remove them. Export a copy when the source matters.

| Action | What it does locally |
| --- | --- |
| Run | Compiles, links and executes the root main package |
| Debug | Runs an instrumented source snapshot with breakpoints, steps, stack and locals |
| Test | Builds and executes tests in project packages, including external `_test` packages and examples with expected output |
| Check | Compiles the root package and its source dependencies without executing a program; this is not Vet |
| Build .wasm | Links and downloads the WASI program without executing it |
| Format | Uses Go's formatter and applies the result only if the source has not changed |
| Stop | Terminates the browser worker immediately and preserves source |

Put input in **Standard input** before Run; EOF follows the supplied text. Output shows success or failure, elapsed time and whether it belongs to the current or an older draft. A run captures the source at its start. Changing code while it runs does not rewrite that result's evidence. Build downloads a WASI binary intended for a compatible runtime, not a native iPhone executable.

The browser uses stock Go 1.27.1 targeting `wasip1/wasm`, with Go's parser and build-constraint selection. Standard-library packages and compatible project/vendor source are supported; text `go:embed` assets can be included. Use **Packages → Prepare packages** for compatible public Go modules declared in `go.mod`, and **Debug** for browser source debugging. Follow the dedicated walkthroughs below. The browser has no cgo, native assembly, OS process spawning, socket networking or race detector. Native npm/React preview instructions apply inside the app.

Budgets: 32 UTF-8 text files, 64 KiB per file, 256 KiB total source, a 30-second execution deadline, up to two minutes per compile/link step, 128 MiB guest linear memory, 4 MiB of cumulative guest-file writes and 1 MiB captured output per program. Compiler memory is separately bounded at 512 MiB. Limits can be reached sooner on a constrained browser. Stop also cancels tool preparation; a later action recreates the worker and reuses verified cached assets.

**Export ZIP** downloads the current source tree. **Import ZIP / JSON** accepts a source ZIP or an earlier GopherForge JSON source copy after validation and replacement confirmation. A ZIP may contain a single enclosing project folder. Binary files, unsafe paths, file/folder collisions and archives over the text-source budgets are rejected. Import does not install dependencies or run code. Browser draft persistence is convenience storage, not an account backup.

The desktop layout keeps a searchable, collapsible file tree beside the editor and a resizable lower panel. Use a file’s action menu to rename, duplicate, download, copy its path or delete it; drag a file onto a folder to move it. Find, editor font size and line wrapping are in the file header. On narrow screens, show the explorer to select a file, then hide it for editing.

sections.title: Browser debugger: breakpoints, steps, stack and locals
sections.body:
Choose **Debug** to pause before the first executable project statement. Click a dot in the Go gutter to add a breakpoint. Blank-line breakpoints bind to the next executable statement in that file. The Debug panel lists breakpoints and highlights the executing line. Use **Continue**, **Step into**, **Step over**, **Step out**, **Pause** or **Stop**. Ordinary Run and Debug are separate browser actions.

For a small exercise, open **Functions & tests** and debug `double(21)`. Step into the call to see `n = 21`, inspect the `double` and `main` stack frames, then Continue to output `42`. Select a frame to reveal its source; captured local values belong to the current frame. Large values have bounded summaries.

The original project compiles first. Checkpoints are inserted into temporary compiler input, leaving saved source unchanged. The editor is read-only during debugging; a collaborator’s source change stops the debug snapshot. Stop terminates the worker, including a call that never reaches another checkpoint. Paused time is excluded from the 30-second execution budget; an abandoned pause expires after 30 minutes.

This teaching debugger steps project Go source. It does not step vendor or standard-library code, evaluate watch expressions, change variables, provide conditional breakpoints or stream stdout while paused. Instrumentation affects timing and allocation. A browser must support cross-origin isolation and SharedArrayBuffer; an unsupported browser shows an explanation rather than starting an ordinary run.

sections.title: Prepare verified public Go dependencies in the browser
sections.body:
Declare an exact public version in `go.mod`, open **Packages** and choose **Prepare packages**. For example:

```go
module playground

go 1.27.1

require github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0
```

Then import `github.com/google/uuid` in your Go program. Preparation downloads public module metadata and archives from `proxy.golang.org`, resolves the required version graph using Go version ordering, verifies `h1:` directory hashes and writes matching `go.sum` entries. Missing checksum entries are authenticated by Go’s official checksum database client against the pinned `sum.golang.org` signing key, including signed tree and inclusion/consistency proofs. Existing `go.sum` entries must match downloaded bytes. A mismatch stops preparation.

The Packages panel lists selected modules and their checksums. The prepared source is cached separately from your editable project. Run, Test, Check, Build and Debug reuse that tree only while `go.mod` and `go.sum` match. After changing either file, prepare again. If source changes during preparation, its newer draft is kept and you are asked to retry.

Public module providers receive module names/versions, your IP and normal request metadata, not the project source or stdin. Downloaded source is verified before compilation. Compatible modules still must support Go/WASI: no cgo, native assembly, sockets or process spawning. Private modules, credentials, `replace` directives, local replacements and `go.work` are unsupported. Go requirements newer than 1.27 are rejected.

Preparation is bounded to 24 selected module paths, 64 graph nodes, 12 MiB per ZIP, 64 MiB expanded archive data, and 512 retained dependency files / 8 MiB text. These dependency files are separate from the editable-source budget. Exported source ZIPs contain your project and manifests; another browser prepares dependencies again. Preparation never runs module code or package scripts.

sections.title: Encrypted live rooms: simultaneous edits and recovery
sections.body:
Choose **Share → Room type → Encrypted → Create one-hour room**. Choose a nickname before sharing or joining. Its small cursor label stays visible without hovering, and **Room → Change nickname** updates it. Recent changes show who edited which files; these are participant-reported labels, not a verified authorship record.

Share the **Edit** link for live changes or **View** for read-only source. Source text uses Yjs CRDT merging, stable file identities and shared cursors. Simultaneous edits are merged; a concurrent rename keeps the same file text. If file names collide, both copies remain under a conflict name. Deleted shared files can be restored from the Room panel.

The browser encrypts document updates, output and participant/cursor state with AES-256-GCM. The key stays in the link fragment and is not sent to the relay. The relay sees encrypted packets, room/role identifiers, sizes, timing and ordinary network metadata. Anyone with the complete link and key has that role until expiry or owner closure. The site serves the browser code, so this protects room content in transit/storage at the relay rather than protecting against a malicious replacement website or compromised participant.

Edits are retained locally during a temporary disconnection and merged on reconnect. Server-side history is periodically compacted with a revision check. A room normally expires after one hour, allows up to 12 active participants and may end earlier on a server restart. Export your project before clearing browser storage or leaving work for later. Local recovery data is ordinary browser storage, not an encrypted disk backup.

Run, Test and Debug always require a local button press. Shared results include the reporting participant and a source fingerprint; old-source results remain identified. View participants can run their local copy but cannot publish edits or results. A remote edit, cursor update or room reconnection never runs code. Keep original source copies when a merged project exceeds the compiler’s 32-file / 256-KiB editable-source limit; recovery copies remain exportable.

App Store 1.3.2 and remote MCP clients use the separate **Compatible** room type. The private TestFlight native 1.3.3 build adds encrypted rooms using the browser’s Yjs/AES-GCM protocol; that build is still in preparation. Remote MCP is not given the encryption key. Choose the compatible type explicitly when following the [MCP setup guide](/guide/mcp). Its revision checks and plaintext relay are described there; switching room types requires leaving the current room while keeping your source.

**Connect an agent through encrypted MCP.** GopherForge’s own JavaScript companion, `gopherforge-mcp`, runs beside your agent on Node.js 22+. It uses the same encrypted room protocol as this browser and native 1.3.3. Setup asks for an agent nickname and the full encrypted Edit/View link, then stores it privately on that machine. Read/write calls, named cursors, change history and reported Output stay encrypted on the relay. A Run/Test request appears in Recent changes; a person still presses the local button. Your MCP host and AI provider can read decrypted tool results. Follow the [complete encrypted MCP and npm setup](/guide/mcp#encrypted-setup). This companion does not require Go or a Node installation on iPhone/iPad. The remote HTTPS MCP remains a separate compatible-room path; never send an encrypted link/key to it.

sections.title: Native Playground 1.3.3: named live collaboration and local tools
sections.body:
**Included in 1.3.3 (55), available in private Internal QA TestFlight; not publicly released.** App Store 1.3.2 retains compatible MCP rooms and its existing full workspace. This section describes the new native implementation.

Open **Projects → Playground → Room & AI connection**. Choose **Encrypted · live editing** for browser/new-native participants or **Compatible · MCP / older apps** for a remote assistant or released native app. Creating a room or opening its link asks for a nickname. Change it in room controls; it appears beside your cursor, in participants, recent changes and newly reported results. A nickname is a display label, not an account or verified identity.

Encrypted rooms merge simultaneous text changes, keep stable file identities through rename/edit races and preserve conflicting copies. The native client uses the same bundled Yjs document and AES-256-GCM packet format as the browser. The key stays in the link fragment. Source, results and cursor/name state are encrypted before upload; the relay still receives capabilities, packet sizes, timing and network metadata. **Recover deleted files** restores shared tombstones. Export/save a project copy before expiry, leaving a room or clearing storage.

Use **Run here**, **Test here**, **Debug**, **Check**, **Format** and **Prepare packages** deliberately. Debug pauses at the first project statement or saved breakpoint and offers Continue, Step Into/Over/Out, stack locations and bounded locals. The editor is read-only during execution; a collaborator’s source change stops a debug snapshot. Native Stop acts at a project checkpoint and is not an immediate interrupt for arbitrary dependency code or an ordinary tight loop.

Declare public Go module versions in `go.mod`, then choose **Prepare packages**. Downloaded vendor source is kept separately on this device and is not inserted into the shared editable tree. Matching prepared source can be reused after relaunch; changing `go.mod` or `go.sum` requires preparation again. Retained dependencies are bounded to 512 files / 8 MiB. Native module/archive compatibility still applies. Preparation and formatting preserve a newer draft instead of overwriting it. A downloaded package is not executed until a local execution action.

Encrypted-room Run/Test/Debug results carry a source fingerprint and the reporting nickname. Compatible runs retain source revisions. View participants can inspect source and run a private local copy, while source edits and result publication remain disabled. Neither a remote edit, cursor, link, reconnection nor MCP request starts the compiler. Keep the app foregrounded for live updates. Native saved recovery data uses protected app storage; room encryption is separate from at-rest device protection.

For a complete assistant session, follow the [MCP sharing walkthrough](/guide/mcp#encrypted-setup). To learn why these execution, release and recovery boundaries matter, study [Go for DevOps and reliability](/learn/units/devops).

sections.title: Complete course downloads and local DevOps labs
sections.body:
Native **1.3.3 (55)** separates **Go**, **DevOps** and **Interview preparation** into complete packages. Open **Learn → Course downloads** and choose **Download complete course**, or use **Import complete course from Files**. The app validates the entire file before installing it. Opening a lesson never starts a background content download. The public 1.3.2 version retains its bundled curriculum.

Each Go course package includes its explanations, examples, compiler checks, hints, verified answers and related practice. The DevOps package includes 34 teaching readings across four units, six terminal labs and a free terminal playground. Export complete course produces the same versioned file for offline reinstallation; it does not merge personal progress into course content. Remove download keeps progress, bookmarks, learner drafts and lab files. Downloaded course content is excluded from device backups because it can be downloaded again.

The **DevOps** learning area joins command line, containers, Kubernetes and delivery/reliability, including IAM, IaC state and DNS/TLS/HTTP diagnosis. Open **DevOps → Open terminal playground** to try your own commands and scripts. Its files and script persist separately from the guided labs. The local terminal executes a bounded shell subset over private lab files, with quotes, variables, redirects, buffered pipelines, conditions and scripts. Checks inspect resulting files and digests. No host process or network request is available to a lab command; Docker, kubectl, SSH and arbitrary binaries are unavailable. Use your own disposable native environment for those integrations.

Each local lab has source, step, nesting, memory, output and storage limits. **Stop** requests cancellation at the next statement boundary; **Reset lab** restores only that lab’s initial files. These controls do not claim a CPU deadline for arbitrary Go programs elsewhere in the app. [Download complete course files and checksums](/downloads).

faq.question: Does GopherForge compile Go offline?
faq.answer: Yes. The native app bundles Go 1.27.1 and compiles compatible programs on the device. Missing packages and GitHub imports need a connection. Browser Playground also compiles locally after its verified Go tools are downloaded; cached assets do not make the entire website an installed offline app.

faq.question: Is progress shared between the app and website?
faq.answer: No. Native progress is local to the app. Web progress uses storage in the current browser. Continue helps you return within each environment; there is no account-based cross-device synchronization.

faq.question: Can I use MongoDB, Redis, SQL or Kubernetes inside the app?
faq.answer: The lessons explain native Go service workflows. They do not add guest-program networking, database servers, Docker, kubectl or a general shell to the app sandbox.

faq.question: Are Codex, Claude Code or Cursor built into GopherForge?
faq.answer: The course teaches those external tools. Compatible MCP clients can deliberately connect to a shared Playground; they can edit and request a run, but a person must press Run/Test in their browser or native app. Ordinary projects are not automatically sent to an AI provider.

faq.question: Why does a small module ZIP hit the file limit?
faq.answer: The budget counts all non-directory archive entries before platform and source filtering. A compact archive can still exceed 4,000 files. Retrying the unchanged archive does not bypass the budget.

faq.question: Is full npm or Bun available on iPhone?
faq.answer: Version 1.3.1 supports a documented offline npm command subset and a fixed React package catalog. It does not install a full npm/Node runtime, Bun, arbitrary Vite plugins or registry packages.

faq.question: Do I need a separate Debug button?
faq.answer: No. In 1.3.1, Run is ordinary execution when the project has no breakpoints. With a breakpoint, the same Run action automatically prepares the source debugger.

faq.question: Can I run Go in a browser without buying the app?
faq.answer: Yes. The free browser Playground provides local Run, Test, Check, Format and WASI builds. On first use it downloads verified compiler assets. Its source, memory and execution budgets are separate from native projects.

faq.question: Does Stop work in the browser Playground?
faq.answer: Yes. Stop terminates the browser worker and preserves the source. A 30-second deadline also bounds program execution. This does not add a universal Stop to ordinary native Go runs.
